catalog_quote: [p. 17] The word level prosodic system in FWS is more complex than in Witsuwit'en, consisting of lexical tone as well as stress. ... The distribution of tone is unpredictable, hence lexically specified, whereas stress is largely predictable in FWS, as in Witsuwit'en. ... [p. 18] Stems are stressed, relative to affixes. ... [p. 19] Impressionistically, primary stress falls on the initial syllables of the verbs in (27) but on the second syllables of the verbs in (28). The difference is that in (27), the vowel of the peninitial syllable is [ɪ] or [ə] whereas in (28), the vowel of the peninitial syllable is [u] or [a] ... Stress falls on the leftmost syllable in sequences of syllables containing the vowel [ə] or [ɪ] ... Word initial position is therefore a stress attracting position. [p. 20] Finally, high tone syllables also appear to attract stress. ... [p. 22] Across speakers, whether or not the second syllable was open or closed had no significant effect on any of these measures. ... [p. 23] FWS prosody consists of lexical tone and predictable stress. All of the factors which influence stress placement in FWS were confirmed by the instrumental studies: stress is attracted to stem (vs. affix) syllables, to word initial (vs. second) syllables, to syllables containing [u] or [a] (vs. [ə] or [ɪ]), and to H (vs. L) tone stem syllables. More descriptive work is needed to determine the relative ranking of these parameters in case of conflict, as with Witsuwit'en.

sweep_summary: Sekani (seka1250) is not in the catalog; the outside-catalog list names only Hargus 1988 (print-only, unread). The one target item, Hargus 2003 'Prosody in Two Athabaskan Languages of Northern British Columbia' (Glottolog 167806, ANLA CA982H2003), was located as an open ANLA scan with an scanned layer (https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/CA982H2003/Prosody.PDF; the ANLA URL in Glottolog is dead, the record is served by https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/drupal/api/record?identifier=.. and files by search.php?res=..). It is the submitted manuscript of Hargus 2005 (Athabaskan Prosody, 393-423) and gives a first-hand, instrument-backed account of Fort Ware Sekani word stress: lexical tone plus predictable stress attracted to stems over affixes, to word-initial over peninitial syllables in runs of reduced vowels, to peripheral [u a] over [ə ɪ], and to H-tone over L-tone stems; closed syllables irrelevant; ranking under conflict left open; correlates duration and energy (§3.2-3.3, ms pp. 17-24). Also downloaded and read: Hargus 2010 Fort Ware consonant-duration slides (confirms stress as an active phonetic category, cites 'Hargus 2005a, b' for placement), Hargus & Abou 2008 intonation slides and Hargus 2009 boundary-tone slides (intonation only, silent on placement), Hargus 2010 Compass survey (pointer only), and the 2000 Ft. Ware Sekani dictionary draft (tone-only orthography, silent on stress). Discovered but unobtainable: Hargus 2005b 'Stress in polysyllabic morphemes: Sekani and Deg Xinag' (WPAL 5: 39-66; ANLA CA001WP2005 has no file) - high priority; Hargus 1985/1988 dissertation/Garland book (McLeod Lake dialect; Harvard print / HathiTrust search-only) - medium. new_statements.rule_in_words: Fort Ware (Kwadacha) Sekani has contrastive lexical tone and a non-contrastive, largely predictable stress. Stem syllables are stressed relative to prefixes; among prefix syllables, stress goes to the word-initial syllable when the following syllables contain reduced [ə]/[ɪ], but to a peninitial syllable containing full [u]/[a] (quality-sensitive stress); H-tone stems attract stress over L-tone stems (a H prefix before a L stem can take the stress). Coda/closed syllables play no role. The ranking of these four factors under conflict is not established.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Transcribed but not analysed: when primary stress is on the word-initial prefix syllable, the stem carries a secondary-stress mark (e.g. ʔəzə̀s 'dɪnɪˌyìs 'she's softening a hide', p. 19); 'It is possible that the stem bears a secondary stress in (31b)' (p. 20).
new_statements.exceptions: Relative ranking of the four parameters when they conflict is left undetermined ('More descriptive work is needed'). Unanalyzable nouns like kəda ~ xəda 'moose' show initial stress without a synchronic stem; the initial-stressed polysyllabic nouns in (30) ('čaba 'Dolly Varden', 'k'ɪni 'sap', 'dɪdi 'this one') may be historical compounds. Study excluded two speakers whose stems were not tone-minimal pairs.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level. Impressionistic transcriptions of verbs in frame sentences and of citation-form nouns, then instrumental confirmation (duration, energy, pitch; 9 speakers). Stress is described as 'largely a subphonemic property' (typescript p. 5) and 'largely predictable' (p. 17); lexical tone (L marked, H default, plus a derived LH rise) is the contrastive word-level prosody. Closed syllables were tested and found NOT to attract stress (p. 21-22).
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Fort Ware (Kwadacha) Sekani (author's 'FWS'; speakers from Ft. Ware / Kwadacha, BC), one dialect of Sekani seka1250 (no separate Glottolog dialect code known to me). The Glottolog-listed Hargus 1985/1988 monograph (not opened) is the earlier description of Sekani; the quoted 2005 study is a later, dialect-specific instrumental study by the same author.

new_statements.reading: Fort Ware (Kwadacha) Sekani has lexical tone plus predictable, non-contrastive word stress. Stress is morphologically and phonologically conditioned rather than fixed-position: stems beat affixes (no suffix is ever stressed), peripheral vowels [u a] beat reduced [ə ɪ], the word-initial syllable beats the peninitial in runs of reduced syllables (so a four-syllable word of three light prefixes plus stem gets initial + final stress), and H-tone stems beat L-tone stems; closed syllables play no role (unlike Witsuwit'en). The relative ranking of these factors under conflict is explicitly left undetermined. Correlates are duration and energy, not F0. A catalog's classification would be 'morphology-sensitive (stem) + quality/weight-sensitive stress, default leftmost, with tone-to-stress attraction; predictable, no lexical contrast', not a simple positional rule.
